questions.question: Which symptom pattern most strongly supports intermittent claudication from PAD?
choices: Reproducible calf tightness with walking that resolves after rest
Leg swelling that only occurs after eating
Sudden pain with a cold pulseless foot
Burning numbness at night unrelated to activity
questions.explanation: Classic claudication is reproducible exertional muscle discomfort relieved by rest. PAD can also be atypical, so history and examination remain essential.

questions.question: A patient has abrupt severe unilateral leg pain, pallor, coolness, numbness, and absent pedal pulse. What is the best next step?
choices: Arrange routine ABI testing next week
Treat as acute limb ischemia and arrange emergency vascular evaluation
Start a walking program and reassess in a month
Diagnose chronic venous insufficiency
questions.explanation: Sudden pain, pallor, poikilothermia, paresthesia, and pulselessness suggest acute limb ischemia. It is a time-sensitive emergency and routine outpatient testing should not delay transfer.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of an ankle-brachial index in a patient with suspected PAD?
choices: It confirms osteoarthritis
It compares ankle and arm systolic pressures to help detect arterial flow disease
It determines the dose of an anticoagulant
It replaces the foot examination
questions.explanation: ABI is a targeted physiologic test that can support PAD diagnosis. It does not replace examination and may be unreliable with noncompressible arteries.

questions.question: Why might ABI interpretation be limited in a patient with diabetes and chronic kidney disease?
choices: Arterial calcification can make vessels noncompressible
Diabetes always eliminates PAD
Kidney disease prevents pulse palpation
ABI only measures venous flow
questions.explanation: Medial arterial calcification can yield noncompressible vessels and falsely elevated ABI values. Toe pressures or vascular-laboratory assessment may be needed.

questions.question: A patient with diabetes has a painless plantar ulcer, reduced sensation, weak pulses, and erythema. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
choices: A painless ulcer is low risk
This may be a mixed neuropathic, ischemic, and infectious problem requiring prompt coordinated evaluation
Only neuropathy is relevant
Compression should be started without arterial assessment
questions.explanation: Diabetic foot wounds can have overlapping neuropathic, ischemic, and infectious causes. Painlessness may reflect neuropathy rather than safety; assess perfusion and infection urgently.

questions.question: Which finding is most concerning for chronic limb-threatening ischemia?
choices: Mild muscle soreness after a new exercise class
Ischemic rest pain with a nonhealing toe wound
Symmetric varicose veins without ulceration
Brief tingling after sitting cross-legged
questions.explanation: Chronic PAD plus rest pain, nonhealing wound, or gangrene suggests chronic limb-threatening ischemia and warrants urgent vascular and wound-care coordination.

questions.question: Which intervention is best described as treatment for symptomatic PAD rather than simple lifestyle advice?
choices: Structured exercise therapy tailored to safety and function
Avoiding all physical activity
Waiting for a wound before addressing risk
Using a cane without evaluation
questions.explanation: Structured exercise can improve walking performance and quality of life. It should be individualized and does not replace urgent evaluation for rest pain, tissue loss, or acute ischemia.

questions.question: Why is tobacco treatment central in PAD care?
choices: Tobacco exposure only affects the lungs
It accelerates PAD and worsens limb and cardiovascular outcomes
It removes the need for lipid treatment
It makes ABI unnecessary
questions.explanation: Tobacco exposure worsens atherosclerosis and PAD outcomes. Repeated counseling plus evidence-based cessation treatment and follow-up are part of vascular care.

questions.question: Which comparison best distinguishes neurogenic claudication from typical vascular claudication?
choices: Neurogenic symptoms may change with posture and improve with flexion, while vascular claudication is more exertion-linked and rest-relieved
Neurogenic claudication always causes absent pulses
Vascular claudication is relieved only by leaning forward
The two diagnoses cannot coexist
questions.explanation: Spinal stenosis symptoms often vary with posture and may improve with sitting or flexion. PAD more often produces reproducible exertional symptoms relieved by rest, though overlap is common.

questions.question: What is the FNP role when revascularization may be needed for lifestyle-limiting PAD despite medical therapy and exercise?
choices: Select the procedure independently without imaging
Coordinate vascular evaluation while continuing risk reduction and foot care
Stop all antithrombotics before referral
Assume pain is psychological
questions.explanation: Vascular specialists determine anatomy and procedural options. Primary care continues prevention, medication safety, exercise support, foot protection, and closed-loop referral.
